authoredPrompt: This figure is a three-part illustration of a bouncing light pulse seen from two reference frames. Part (a) shows a side view of a space shuttle above a magnified inset: inside a rounded frame an astronaut in an orange suit, labeled Astronaut, floats beside an analog clock reading delta tau, while a Light source drawn as a yellow burst and a Receiver sit side by side beneath a Mirror, with teal arrows carrying the pulse straight up and straight back down over the bracketed vertical distance D. Part (b) shows the same apparatus from outside: three dashed-outline snapshots of the cabin run left to right, and a purple path labeled s goes diagonally up from the source in the left snapshot, labeled Beginning event, to the mirror in the middle snapshot, then down as a second segment s to the receiver in the right snapshot, labeled Ending event. Brackets below give the horizontal shifts L = v delta t / 2 and L, and a standing figure on a tan ground plane is labeled Observer on Earth beside a clock reading delta t. Part (c) reduces the picture to bare geometry, an isosceles triangle whose two slanted sides are each labeled s, divided by a vertical altitude D into right triangles with bases L = v delta t / 2 and L, with s = sqrt(D squared + L squared) written above. Drawing the same pair of events twice makes the two path lengths directly comparable, which is what forces the two recorded times apart.
authoredInteractions:
- Toggle between astronaut frame and Earth frame: learner switches the named observer view; the light path changes from straight up-and-down distance 2D to two diagonal segments 2s while the clocks display delta tau and delta t; the frame dependence of elapsed time becomes clear.
- Slider for shuttle speed v: learner increases or decreases horizontal motion; the cabin snapshots spread apart, L grows, the diagonal light path lengthens, and delta t increases relative to delta tau; the geometric origin of time dilation becomes visible.
- Button sequence through beginning, mirror reflection, and ending event: learner steps the pulse through the three events; the same event markers light up in both apparatus and triangle panels; the shared events explain why the two observers can disagree about path length but not about what happened.
authoredContext:
The analysis of simultaneity shows that Einstein’s postulates imply an important effect: Time intervals have different values when measured in different inertial frames. Suppose, for example, an astronaut measures the time it takes for a pulse of light to travel a distance perpendicular to the direction of his ship’s motion (relative to an earthbound observer), bounce off a mirror, and return (the figure). How does the elapsed time that the astronaut measures in the spacecraft compare with the elapsed time that an earthbound observer measures by observing what is happening in the spacecraft?

Examining this question leads to a profound result. The elapsed time for a process depends on which observer is measuring it. In this case, the time measured by the astronaut (within the spaceship where the astronaut is at rest) is smaller than the time measured by the earthbound observer (to whom the astronaut is moving). The time elapsed for the same process is different for the observers, because the distance the light pulse travels in the astronaut’s frame is smaller than in the earthbound frame, as seen in the figure. Light travels at the same speed in each frame, so it takes more time to travel the greater distance in the earthbound frame.

To quantitatively compare the time measurements in the two inertial frames, we can relate the distances in the figure to each other, then express each distance in terms of the time of travel (respectively either Δt or Δτ) of the pulse in the corresponding reference frame. The resulting equation can then be solved for Δt in terms of Δτ.

The lengths D and L in the figure are the sides of a right triangle with hypotenuse s. From the Pythagorean theorem,

(a) An astronaut measures the time Δτ for light to travel distance 2D in the astronaut’s frame. (b) A NASA scientist on Earth sees the light follow the longer path 2s and take a longer time Δt. (c) These triangles are used to find the relationship between the two distances D and s.

Figure a shows an illustration of an astronaut in the space shuttle observing an analog clock with an elapsed time Delta tau. The details of the clock experiment are also shown as follows: There is a light source, a receiver a short distance to its right, and a mirror centered above them. The vertical distance from the receiver and light source to the mirror is labeled as D. The path of the light from the source, up to the mirror, and back down to the receiver is shown. Figure b shows an observer on earth with an analog clock showing a time interval Delta t. Above the observer are three diagrams showing the clock experiment on the space shuttle at three different times and the path of the light. The light source in the diagram on the left is labeled “beginning event.” The receiver in the diagram on the right is labeled “ending event.” The path of the light forms a straight line going diagonally up and to the right, from the source in the diagram on the left to the mirror in the center diagram, and then another straight line going diagonally down and to the right, from the mirror in the center diagram to the receiver in the diagram on the right. The vertical distance from the receiver to the mirror is labeled D. The horizontal distance from the beginning event to the clock location in the center diagram is labeled L= v Delta t over 2. The horizontal distance from the clock location in the center diagram to the ending event is labeled L. Figure c shows an isosceles triangle with a horizontal base. The triangle is divided by a vertical line from its apex to its base into two identical right triangles with the vertical line forming a side that is shared by the two right triangles. This side is labeled D. The base of the triangle on the left is labeled L= v Delta t over 2. The base of the triangle on the right is labeled L. The hypotenuse of each of the right triangles is labeled s. Above the diagram is the equation s equals the square root of the quantity D squared plus L squared.

discrepancies: The Earth-frame sequence in panel (b) is scaled/positioned too far to the right: the third dashed cabin and ending-event area are mostly clipped in the default screenshot, whereas the source shows all three snapshots fully.
Panel (c) is placed too low and cramped; the triangle base and lower labels sit at or beyond the bottom of the viewBox instead of being cleanly centered with ample whitespace as in the source.

The generated default view adds large event-marker circles on the apparatus, cabin snapshots, and triangle vertices, plus an active-frame caption, which are not present in the source static figure and make it less like a drop-in replacement.
Several panel (b) labels are too small or crowded, especially the beginning-event label and the L = v Δt / 2 bracket label, and the top caption is visibly truncated in the screenshot.
The panel (c) equation is typeset as “s = √ D² + L²” without a clear radical bar or parentheses over the full sum, unlike the source equation s = √(D² + L²).

The shuttle and cabin interiors are simplified compared with the source, losing some recognizable details such as the full detailed shuttle body, windows, exhaust/engines, and the clearer interior clock/light-clock layout.
evaluation.notes: The figure captures the main light-clock panels and has useful working interactions, but the default composition is not a clean source replacement because key right/bottom content is clipped or cramped and extra event overlays clutter the static appearance.
action_items: Rescale or reposition panel (b) so all three dashed cabin snapshots, the D bracket, both L brackets, and the beginning/ending event labels are fully visible at the default speed.
Move panel (c) upward or reduce its size so the full triangle, base line, part label, and lower L labels are not clipped or crowded.
Replace the panel (c) equation with an unambiguous form such as s = √(D² + L²) or draw a proper radical bar over D² + L².
Reduce or hide the large event-marker circles and active-frame caption in the default state so the initial view more closely matches the static textbook figure.
